sources.title: Paul Bettany (The Times interview by Tim Teeman, author repost)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Tim Teeman
sources.locator: Margin Call press interview; paragraphs on school, Matthew, cocaine, therapy, fame (author archive repost of The Times piece)
sources.excerpt: "I was a really bullied kid," ... "My godfather was gay and I would challenge every homophobic comment I heard. Consequently I had the shit kicked out of me because they thought I was gay." ... "It was a heart- breaking, alienating experience. I felt like I was harbouring this huge secret. I was so fragile." ... "I stopped because it was threatening my ability to act: the one thing that gave me self-worth." ... "God yes, four years on and off. In a world absent of Jesus, it's the flawed, but solitary option." ... He remains "full of self-doubt — I do not operate from a place of certainty". ... "But you shouldn't be sustained by other people's adulation. What if it goes away?" ... "I was terrified of reading aloud — it was so humil- iating that I used to hide." ... "I tot- ally fell in love with it the moment I started doing it."
sources.context: Long-form Times interview over lunch in New York, age 40, promoting Margin Call. Covers dyslexia and bullying, Matthew's death at 8 when Paul was 16, early-20s cocaine addiction ("work kept me on an even keel"), the 9/11 phone calls to Connelly, therapy, and fame. Teeman notes it is "all said without self-pity". Also: "Making Margin Call 'was the first amazing artistic experience I'd had in years' ... 'It made me think I can't be a gun for hire any more.'" Text read on the author's archive; the original Times page was not opened. Edit stage (2026-10-30): Also on the cached page: "I used to bunk off and had a lot of revenge fantasies where I thought, 'One day you'll be sorry.'" His desire to act was "absolutely" fuelled by this (Teeman's paraphrase around the quoted word). "Acting became a vocation. I don't remember thinking it was about money until I had kids." When Stellan was born "he took a year and a half off"; he won't name the films "which have made me the most amount of money in the shortest amount of time so I could get back to my family". "I need to be happy, and if that means making films for less money, so be it." "When both were single, September 11 happened" (both had other partners during A Beautiful Mind). His brother's fall "is right there" when his children jump on the couch: "I have to stop myself from shouting, 'Stop it.'" "His parents were both former actors."

sources.title: Paul Bettany interview: this time it's serious (The Telegraph, Celia Walden)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Celia Walden
sources.locator: Full article via Wayback raw capture; paragraphs on lateness, son's birth and money, school bullying, 9/11, addiction, death
sources.excerpt: 'I have a pathological fear of being late' ... 'Suddenly I thought to myself, "---- all this. The world is precarious and I'm going to make my children as safe as possible – with dough." And I went about doing that. It was ludicrous, of course, because they were safe. ... but there I was hammering bits of wood against the window as though there were a zombie apocalypse coming. It sounds neurotic, but it's not, because the tap can turn off.' ... 'I was a city boy and I was terrified of everyone' ... 'My experience of addiction was very much linked to a lack of foundation, feeling rootless and not knowing who I was' ... 'I felt so uneducated. Those people were supersized to me and I was always trying to proximate the way they constructed their sentences.' ... 'I worry about death in general a lot.' ... 'It was constant,' ... 'I was bullied about everything, from the way I looked to the fact that my father had been a dancer.' ... 'I can tell you right now that I'm not feeling particularly guarded.' ... 'I thought to myself, "Why have I been calling this woman for three days?" Then suddenly it dawned on me.' ... Auditions 'were always fine, because I would never sight read, I would just learn things by heart. Right up until the read-through for A Beautiful Mind, I was still learning my lines by heart and pretending to read my part. Now I've stopped doing that. It was the anxiety that made my dyslexia worse.'
sources.context: Interview at the Chateau Marmont while shooting Transcendence, promoting Blood (2013). Walden reports he tries not to be away from family for longer than two weeks, that after 9/11 he rang Connelly for days ("Why have I been calling this woman for three days?"), and that the marriage gave him "a certainty that was new to me". She also reports his father "aged 75 ... announced his bisexuality", which conflicts with Bettany's later "came out at 63". The bullying at Chancellors school predates Matthew's death. Walden was warned he would not discuss his brother that day. Walden also reports the money plan included buying 'the 100-acre farm in Vermont he wanted his children to have as a weekend retreat', that his parents divorced in 1993, that he arrived 'two minutes late, having called to say he may be delayed', and that Master and Commander was 'a global box-office hit' in 2003. The 'It blew the family apart' line is quoted as something he 'has said'. Edit stage (2026-10-30): Also: 'Growing up, I'd always loved acting, but fame? Well I suppose I did want it in a childish, revenge fantasy kind of way'; the bullying 'set off the childish motor in me'; 'I know great actors whom nothing has ever happened for' follows the tap line; after Margin Call 'I had made some bad choices. I decided I wasn't going to do that any more'; Walden lists Wimbledon (2004), Firewall (2006), The Da Vinci Code and Priest among his studio-shaped roles; 'His parents' marriage buckled under the strain of the trauma, the pair eventually divorcing in 1993'; family: 'a younger brother, Matthew, and an older sister, Sarah'; 'his mother, Anne, had given up acting years earlier'. The 'certainty that was new to me' fragment sits inside Walden's sentence about 'Their romance', and the security frame is partly hers: the standfirst says he 'followed the Hollywood dollar for the sake of his family's security' and she writes 'One can only ever guess at a person's motivations, but it seems likely that in his relationship with Connelly, Bettany finally had the foundations he'd craved as a young man.' The article treats that as her inference, not his.

sources.title: Paul Bettany on How He Rekindled His Love for Acting (Daily Actor, relaying The Guardian)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, quoted from a Guardian interview
sources.locator: Second and third paragraphs quoting the Guardian Blood interview
sources.excerpt: "Acting used to be somewhere I could put loads of terrible feelings and bad experiences and try to make something creative out of them. But then I married and had children and everything got eclipsed. I know how precarious life can be, so I then had a period when I was making as much money as I could, so my children would be safe. Then I made a film called Margin Call, which was shot in two weeks on a low budget."
sources.context: Daily Actor summary of a 2013 Guardian interview about Blood. The Guardian original could not be opened (crawler blocked), so this is a secondary relay; the same safety-through-money account appears independently in S02 two weeks earlier and in S01.

sources.title: Interview: Paul Bettany On Creation (CinemaBlend)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany
sources.locator: Q&A answer on whether he was nervous acting with Connelly
sources.excerpt: My heartbeat tends to lower when cameras are on. I tend to get much calmer. I'm anxious in everyday life. I'm anxious about my kids' health, my health, whether I"m going to get the job I want, the chicken's going to turn out all right, the dog's going to poop in front of the paparazzi.
sources.context: Roundtable-style junket interview for Creation, in which he played Darwin opposite Connelly. Delivered with jokes; the interviewer calls him "as lively and funny as you might expect". He adds that on Master and Commander he could hold bugs once the camera rolled though he "fucking hate[s] bugs".

sources.title: Paul Bettany on why his directorial debut is about homelessness (The Independent, Kaleem Aftab)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Kaleem Aftab
sources.locator: Paragraphs on the film's theme, busking, and his father
sources.excerpt: "But I didn't want to make a film about homelessness," he insists. "I wanted it to be about judgment." ... "It's just that people are eminently forgivable." ... "My father, who has just died, was a very religious man," says Bettany. "I'm not. I was raised a Catholic and he used to say this thing whenever we passed a homeless person, 'There but for the grace of God, go I.' Although I'm not a religious man, I love that sentence. There is an admission of how easily it can be us."
sources.context: Interview about Shelter (2014), which he wrote and directed and which stars Connelly. The story was inspired by a homeless couple outside his New York home. He says his busking past probably fed the film but "I didn't want it to become part of a narrative in discussing the film". Connelly, he says, "is incredibly honest about my artistic endeavours – brutally so." Edit stage (2026-10-30): The busking quote in full: "I didn't want it to become part of a narrative in discussing the film. Because I think it's a sticky subject. It's a bit like politicians kissing babies." Used as pre-2026 evidence of guarding rather than displaying personal pain.

sources.title: Paul Bettany talks 'Uncle Frank' and his own closeted father (Windy City Times)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany
sources.locator: Q&A answer to whether he was reluctant to accept the role
sources.excerpt: But the first question I had for Alan was "Why me?," and I [followed that] with "Should I even do this?" ... My father, because of the dogma of Catholicism, went back into the closet. He was arguably with the love of his life and when my father died—in my arms!—I found in his pocket a glass vial of Andy's ashes. ... My father had some beautifully curated stories and anecdotes, but I never really got to know him because he didn't live his life in an authentic way.
sources.context: Phone Q&A for Uncle Frank (2020), in which he plays a closeted gay professor. He says he asked himself whether it was "morally correct" to take the role and whether he had "the energy" to "think of some dark moments in your life". He and director Alan Ball found they shared "early traumas in our lives and deaths of our siblings". Edit stage (2026-10-30): The question that prompted 'Why me?' was about the view that only LGBTQ actors should play LGBTQ roles; he said 'That wasn't the only reason I was reluctant' and named whether it was 'morally correct' and whether he had 'the energy' to 'think of some dark moments in your life'. A Windy City Times editor's note dates Thane's coming out to the early 1990s, with Paul's parents divorcing afterward.

sources.title: Paul Bettany Says His Gay Father Went Back Into The Closet in His 80s (Out, relaying Total Film and NewNowNext)

sources.title: Paul Bettany says having his texts with Johnny Depp about Amber Heard made public was 'a strange moment' (Yahoo Entertainment, relaying The Independent)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany (via The Independent)
sources.locator: Paragraphs quoting the Independent interview
sources.excerpt: "It was a strange moment," he said of being involved in Depp's legal battle. "What was strange about it was you suddenly have one of the most scabrous newspapers in London and their lawyers poring through your texts for the last 10 years. Can you imagine what it would be like, honestly, to have a bunch of lawyers go through every one of your emails and texts for 10 years? All I can tell you was that it was an unpleasant feeling." ... "I don't feel that I signed some Faustian pact with the devil when I became an actor to give away all my privacy."
sources.context: Secondary relay of a December 2021 Independent interview (original not opened). He says "I think that I just pour fuel on the fire" by discussing it, and recalls a filmed subway argument with Connelly that led to divorce rumours reaching his children's school. Edit stage (2026-10-30): The relay also reports: 'A British court ultimately dismissed Depp's claim that it was libelous for the newspaper to refer to him as a "wife beater" in light of ex-wife Amber Heard's allegations of abuse.' It dates the texts to 2013 and 2014 and calls Depp his 'Mortdecai and The Tourist co-star'.

sources.title: Paul Bettany says it was 'embarrassing' to have texts with Johnny Depp shared during court trial (Insider, via Yahoo)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany (via The Times); text messages read in court
sources.locator: Article body: text exchange as read in court; Times quotes; 2016 tweet
sources.excerpt: In a series of texts, Depp wrote, "Let's burn Amber!!!" to which Bettany responded: "Having thought it through I don't think we should burn Amber — she's delightful company and easy on the eye, plus I'm not sure she's a witch. We could of course try the English course of action in these predicaments — we do a drowning test. Thoughts?" ... "We live in a world without context," he said. "I didn't know Johnny when he was married to Amber. I knew him before. But we hadn't spoken for years." ... "I know how this works. Anything that you say is oxygen for a fire. And there's just no fucking fire," he added. ... In a tweet in 2016, Bettany said: "Known Johnny Depp for years and through several relationships. He's the sweetest, kindest, gentlest man that I've ever known. Just saying." ... Depp had strenuously denied all claims that he was violent toward Heard.
sources.context: Insider report on a February 2022 Times interview given before The Collaboration opened at the Young Vic. The 2013 messages were read in Depp's 2020 UK libel case against The Sun's publisher (which Depp lost) and resurfaced in his 2022 US trial against Amber Heard. The wording of the texts varies slightly between outlets. The Times original was not opened. Edit stage (2026-10-30): Fuller Times quote: "I didn't know Johnny when he was married to Amber. I knew him before. But we hadn't spoken for years. During the marriage, I didn't know them. So I wasn't around for any of that." He called the court episode "embarrassing" and "a very surreal moment". He does not date when contact stopped; the article quotes him rather than paraphrasing a timeline. Insider also reports that in November 2020 Depp lost the libel case over a 2018 headline calling him a "wife beater", that Judge Andrew Nicol referred to 14 incidents, and that Heard had accused Depp of physical abuse in 2016.

sources.title: Paul Bettany on fame, playing the game, and staying sane (Gentleman's Journal, Joseph Bullmore)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Joseph Bullmore
sources.locator: Hour-long Zoom interview; sections on emotion access, fame, isolation, "Finish strong", neurosis
sources.excerpt: "Some people have amazing access to their emotions, and can switch them on like that," ... "And I'm just not good enough to do that." ... "if I find myself in a scene that requires that, I find myself picking at scabs that I'd rather not pick at," ... "But it's spurious and I have watched it, with myself, come and go — it's an untrustworthy thing. You shouldn't find solace in it." ... "You're certainly not meeting the actual me, and I'm not meeting who you really are." ... "What I have realised is that I do better than I think in isolation," he says. "I'm quite convivial and social, and so I'm always surprised to see how well I do with my own company. I feel like I shouldn't have the personal resources to be on my own at all. I feel like I should fall apart more than I do. But I don't." ... "It's irritatingly industrious of me. But I have that ethos myself, when I'm up at work and tired and against it." ... "I'm not any less neurotic now, by the way" he says before we go. "I'm just better at hiding it." ... "you've only ever seen this really carefully curated public persona" ... "And it's like: What am I doing? What am I doing! What the hell am I doing! Sat here in front of a graveyard, thinking about dead people in my life?" ... "That's something that makes me feel less alone and alienated in the world" ... "I'm quite convivial and social, and so I'm always surprised to see how well I do with my own company. I feel like I shouldn't have the personal resources to be on my own at all."
sources.context: Interview from a cabin near his Vermont house for the film of The Collaboration. Also: Talking about acting "is like talking about sex"; the Lennon lyric "makes me feel less alone and alienated in the world"; a fan asked for a selfie while he stood crying after hearing his father was gravely ill. The journalist calls Stellan "the oldest" of the children; Kai, Connelly's son, is older. The 'less alone and alienated' line is about John Lennon's lyric from 'Mother', which the writer calls the most moving lyric Bettany can think of. The Warhol line describes why he first refused the role. The sweatshirt detail is the writer's report of what Bettany 'has said in interviews before'. Edit stage (2026-10-30): The 'actual me' line is two-way and about fan encounters ('I'm not meeting you, and you're not meeting me. Or: You're certainly not meeting the actual me, and I'm not meeting who you really are'); the edit no longer uses it. The isolation answer turns: he does 'better than I think in isolation' and adds 'I feel like I should fall apart more than I do. But I don't.' The 'not good enough' line follows a comparison: 'Some people have amazing access to their emotions, and can switch them on like that'.

sources.title: Paul Bettany on playing Warhol, family ghosts, and how therapy 'saved' him (The Daily Beast, Tim Teeman, author repost)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Tim Teeman
sources.locator: Zoom interview during the Broadway run of The Collaboration; sections on fear, bullying, father, therapy, work ethic, career slump, Depp, citizenship
sources.excerpt: "For instance, with Andy Warhol, it's his fear. I was very bullied as a schoolkid, and I remember the world feeling like a frightening place. I try to remember that in me." ... "I wouldn't take part in any of the homophobic banter around me, and the consequence of that, well you can imagine… I sort of refused to bend on that." ... "It's more that I have a really strong work ethic. ... The thing I could control was being the most prepared person auditioning that day." ... "I couldn't just fall apart. What was making me feel safe and relevant was my career, rather like Warhol. Then my children came along, and all of that disappeared like mist." ... "We had kids, suddenly we had a fucking mortgage. I thought, what if this thing comes tumbling down?" ... "I said to him, 'Look, this town is full of second and third acts, and you should mind your fucking manners.' I walked out. My legs went because I acted so tough!" ... "When I'm away from them too much I begin to revert to older habits," ... "I am so much less certain and definitive about things." ... "I refuse to put more fuel on this fire that's just been really unpleasant." ... "It's more that I have a really strong work ethic." ... "He said, 'Well that was only physical for a very short time.'" ... "While I understand therapy is like having a chronic injury where you need to constantly be doing physical therapy and massage or you lean back into old patterns of behavior, I have also discovered it has really saved me." ... "My father had been a dancer and actor."
sources.context: Daily Beast interview reposted on the author's site. Also: therapy "absolutely saved me" and is "like having a chronic injury" needing upkeep or "you lean back into old patterns"; "I was very lost for a number of years, but there were always something that saved me or people that saved me"; politics occupies him "to an unhealthy extent"; he took US citizenship because he "was tired of getting shouted down on Twitter for having an opinion". Teeman reports the father died "aged 86 in 2015" and Bettany says his father came out "when he was 63". Bettany declined to discuss the Depp texts further. Teeman reports Thane became 'a first-time father at 42'. The 'safe and relevant' line refers to his career before his children arrived ('Then my children came along, and all of that disappeared like mist'), not to the post-2008 slump; the draft does not use it. Edit stage (2026-10-30): Also: "I fell into acting" (after wanting to be a guitar player); "Paul, you're done in this business. It's over for you" from a producer he had turned down years before; "it turns out when he was pitching me to Kevin Feige, I was already playing the voice of J.A.R.V.I.S. Feige asked Josh, 'Well can he play a superhero?' And Josh able to show one of these movies I thought was the nadir of my career to say, 'Yes he can!'"; the 'most prepared person' quote continues 'I was the person they remembered'; 'judging yourself only though the praise of others' is listed among 'terrible, terrible things'; 'For instance, with Andy Warhol, it's his fear. I was very bullied as a schoolkid, and I remember the world feeling like a frightening place. I try to remember that in me.'; 'My mother was a singer.'

sources.excerpt: "I hadn't spoken to Johnny in years when that happened and I haven't spoken to him since. I was being painted as this close friend of a guy I hadn't spoken to in years and, honestly, amid all the s--- two celebrities threw at each other, that bit was the most odd," he said. "So I decided to say nothing because, I think, people know me. I've been married 23 years [to actress Jennifer Connelly] and, for what I do, I live an incredibly quiet life," Bettany added. "Everybody kind of thought this is probably a nothing burger — and left it alone." ... On the stand, Depp said the exchange was a riff on Monty Python and was never meant literally. ... In 2022, a Virginia jury largely sided with Depp and awarded him $15 million. ... Heard won one of her three counterclaims and was awarded $2 million. The two settled in December 2022 ... Bettany replied in the same mock-medieval spirit.
sources.context: Secondary report of a VisionQuest-era Times interview (original not opened). Gulf News notes the 2016 X/Twitter post praising Depp "appears to have disappeared when Bettany left the platform", and that he discussed the texts with The Times in 2022. Other 2026 outlets report boycott calls against VisionQuest over the texts. Gulf News does not say in which trial Depp gave the Monty Python testimony; the draft says only that he told the court. Edit stage (2026-10-30): Gulf News also reports: 'The texts date to 2013, when Depp and Bettany were working together. The two appeared in three films between 2010 and 2015'; Depp and Heard 'began dating in 2013, married in 2015, and split the following year'; and that what bothered Bettany most 'wasn't the jokes' but being presented as Depp's close friend. 'So I decided to say nothing' follows directly on 'that bit was the most odd', so it refers to not contesting the close-friend portrayal; the article quotes it in that order and no longer sets it against his 2021-2022 remarks.

sources.context: Sibling Revelry episode released 13 October 2026, the day before VisionQuest premiered; hosts Kate and Oliver Hudson, Bettany speaking from New York. Audio downloaded from the public RSS enclosure and transcribed locally (whisper small.en for the whole episode; the quoted clips re-transcribed with large-v3-turbo, which agreed). The conversation has three voices and no speaker labels, so only lines that answer a question put to Bettany are attributed; nearby remarks about actors needing approval and validation are not attributed to him. Both models heard "couldn't turn very negative things into something creative" where the sense suggests "could"; that phrase is not quoted. The 9/11 account here says "about 48 hours" of calling; the 2013 Telegraph has "three days". He attributes the lyric "Mother, you had me, but I never had you" to "Sean Lennon"; it is John Lennon's "Mother". He says his father came out "at 63", consistent with his 2020 and 2022 accounts. Draft stage (2026-10-30): the clips for career worry, safety net, punctuality, the mask answer and 9/11 were transcribed a third time with whisper medium.en. Quoted spans are words all three models share, or (for 'being on time' and 'second string to your bow') two of three where the third is a clear mishearing ('one time', 'bone'); the bow phrase is paraphrased, not quoted. Quotations drop spoken false starts and stutters ('I can do, I can do', 'the, the trauma and, and, and drama'). Small.en and turbo disagree on 'which bits were me' / 'which bits for me' (medium: 'were me'), so that clause is paraphrased. These are machine transcriptions, not a human listen. Edit stage (2026-10-30): Stable locators: RSS enclosure https://podtrac.com/pts/redirect.mp3/pscrb.fm/rss/p/traffic.omny.fm/d/clips/e73c998e-6e60-432f-8610-ae210140c5b1/65e41873-3a0f-4dd4-a8f5-b0a000dc39b5/b105812c-a5d9-4447-82cb-b4e2002b8273/audio.mp3 (episode length 2559 s per feed); the article cites 13:44 for the safety-net answer and 28:10 for the mask answer. The 'safety net' line is said jokingly ('which is hilarious ... or acting being a rock and roll star doesn't work out'). In the mask answer Kate Hudson first offers 'disappearing there would be a place' and he says 'I think so'; the answer then gives two reasons in order: drama school 'gave me a place that I [could] turn very negative things into something creative' (all models hear 'couldn't'; paraphrased, not quoted) 'And there was always a mask that I could hide behind'. Punctuality (20:50-21:15): he credits drama-school training to arrive by 'the half' before 'an absolute fascist about being on time'. Brother (23:22-24:10): the guilt line is followed by 'everybody is sort of dropped into a maze by their childhood' and 'a lot of time, you know, a lot of therapy'. 9/11 (41:24-43:18): 'I was with somebody. She was with somebody' refers to the A Beautiful Mind period; after the calls they married after he shot Master and Commander and saw her at weekends. Still machine transcription; no human listen has been done.

claims.claim: Bettany's younger brother Matthew died at age 8 after falling from a tennis pavilion roof at the school where their father taught; Paul was 16, and he says the death "blew the family apart".
claims.passage: Then, when he was 16, his eight-year-old brother Matthew fell from the roof of a tennis pavilion and died.
claims.inference: A dated, repeatedly told formative loss; it establishes the circumstance every later safety-seeking choice has to be weighed against.
claims.alternative: Grief and trauma alone can produce lifelong hypervigilance in any type; this event cannot by itself show type.

claims.claim: In October 2026 he said Matthew fell from a building "that I had taught him how to climb", leaving "an enormous amount of guilt to work through".
claims.passage: Matthew "fell off a building that I had taught him how to climb. So there was an enormous amount of guilt to work through on that."
claims.inference: Adds a self-blame strand that later interviews show being worked through in therapy; useful as a late, specific disclosure rather than as type proof.
claims.alternative: Survivor guilt after a sibling death is common and circumstantial; it does not discriminate between 6 and 4.

claims.claim: He describes fear as predating the brother's death: bullied constantly at his Hertfordshire school, he says "I was a city boy and I was terrified of everyone".
claims.passage: "I was a city boy and I was terrified of everyone," Bettany told the Telegraph. The bullying at his Hertfordshire school was "constant," and it covered "everything, from the way I looked to the fact that my father had been a dancer."
claims.inference: Fearfulness reported before the 16-year-old's trauma weakens a trauma-only explanation of his later vigilance and supports an anxious baseline.
claims.alternative: A new boy bullied at a hostile school has situational reasons for fear; the article says so in the next sentence. Fearfulness under bullying is not type-specific.

claims.claim: At school he refused to join homophobic banter and challenged it, and was beaten for it; he says "I sort of refused to bend on that."
claims.passage: His godfather was gay, and he challenged the homophobic talk around him. "Consequently I had the shit kicked out of me because they thought I was gay,"
claims.inference: Taking a costly stand for a threatened in-group (his gay godfather, father's world) fits a loyal, counterphobic Six pattern of standing firm against the threat.
claims.alternative: Could equally reflect Four identification with outsiders, or simple moral conviction; it does not by itself discriminate.

claims.claim: In his early twenties he became addicted to cocaine, which he linked to "a lack of foundation, feeling rootless and not knowing who I was".
claims.passage: "My experience of addiction was very much linked to a lack of foundation, feeling rootless and not knowing who I was."
claims.inference: His own diagnosis of the addiction is about missing foundation, i.e. security and grounding.
claims.alternative: "Not knowing who I was" is also classic Four identity language; this passage cuts both ways.

claims.claim: He says he quit cocaine because it threatened his ability to act, "the one thing that gave me self-worth".
claims.passage: He quit, he told The Times, "because it was threatening my ability to act: the one thing that gave me self-worth."
claims.inference: Work functioned as a stabilising structure; he chose the structure over the drug.
claims.alternative: A Three reading (worth through work) also fits this line; the later rejection of praise as a measure (C12) weighs against that.

claims.claim: After the 9/11 calls he and Connelly married on 1 January 2003 in Scotland without having lived together first; the Telegraph quotes him saying the romance gave him "a certainty that was new to me".
claims.passage: They married in Scotland on January 1, 2003, without having lived together first. In the Telegraph's account, the romance gave him "a certainty that was new to me."
claims.inference: A threat to someone he cared about produced repeated calling and then a commitment he describes in terms of certainty. The phoning itself is ordinary and is not used as type evidence; the certainty remark is the type-relevant part.
claims.alternative: Crisis-driven romantic clarity is common in many types. The 'certainty' fragment sits inside Walden's sentence about their romance, and the security/foundations frame was first proposed by the Telegraph writer (standfirst and 'it seems likely ... the foundations he'd craved'), so it is not an independent discovery. Marrying quickly is not typical Six testing.

claims.claim: When his son was born he decided "the world is precarious" and set out to make his children "as safe as possible – with dough", taking studio jobs for money; he called it "hammering bits of wood against the window as though there were a zombie apocalypse coming".
claims.passage: And I went about doing that. It was ludicrous, of course, because they were safe. My wife and I make enough money to ensure their safety, but there I was hammering bits of wood against the window as though there were a zombie apocalypse coming. It sounds neurotic, but it's not, because the tap can turn off.
claims.inference: The clearest repeated, costly choice: he traded artistic preference for financial security, while recognising the threat was exaggerated. This is the main Six discriminator against Four.
claims.alternative: Ordinary parental prudence, and an actor's incentive to justify commercial roles in hindsight; a Four could make the same trade under pressure.

claims.claim: After making Margin Call (2011) cheaply, he said "I can't be a gun for hire any more" and that the film reminded him what he loved about acting.
claims.passage: Making it, he told The Times, "was the first amazing artistic experience I'd had in years," and "It made me think I can't be a gun for hire any more."
claims.inference: Shows the security strategy was revisable once a safer footing existed; meaning returned after safety.
claims.alternative: This return to artistic meaning is the strongest Four-compatible turn in the record.

claims.claim: He frames his professional discipline as control over uncertainty: "I have a really strong work ethic" and "The thing I could control was being the most prepared person auditioning that day."
claims.passage: The thing I could control was being the most prepared person auditioning that day.
claims.inference: Preparation as a hedge against what cannot be controlled, repeated across 2013, 2022 and 2026.
claims.alternative: Professional craft norms and British punctuality; Olsen's "precise" remark could reflect training rather than anxiety.

claims.claim: He describes himself as anxious in everyday life but calmer once cameras roll (2010).
claims.passage: My heartbeat tends to lower when cameras are on. I tend to get much calmer. I'm anxious in everyday life.
claims.inference: Consistent first-person anxiety across 2010, 2012 and 2022, including the observation that he becomes calmer once the camera (action) starts.
claims.alternative: Self-deprecating anxiety talk is also a British comic register and a junket habit; self-report cannot show the motive is core.

claims.claim: He treats fame and praise as unreliable supports: "What if it goes away?" (2012); "it's an untrustworthy thing. You shouldn't find solace in it" (2022); judging yourself by others' praise is one of the "terrible, terrible things" about the job.
claims.passage: In 2012 he told The Times that "you shouldn't be sustained by other people's adulation. What if it goes away?" A decade later fame was "an untrustworthy thing"
claims.inference: Distrust of an external support, framed as a security question, argues against a Three reading and fits Six scepticism.
claims.alternative: A Four also distrusts fame because it misrecognises the "actual me" (C18).

claims.claim: He says he worries about death "a lot" (2013).
claims.passage: "I worry about death in general a lot" (Telegraph, 2013)
claims.inference: Threat-scanning focused on the safety of loved ones, consistent with a Six attention pattern.
claims.alternative: Directly traceable to Matthew's fall; circumstance may explain it fully. The Telegraph writer's sense that it might exist even without the loss is impression, not evidence.

claims.claim: After the 2008 crash he made films that "helped us financially", worried "what if this thing comes tumbling down?", and then could not get a job for about two years.
claims.passage: he made films that "helped us financially. We had kids, suddenly we had a fucking mortgage. I thought, what if this thing comes tumbling down? For around two years I couldn't get a job."
claims.inference: Explicit safety language attached to work and money, a decade after C08.
claims.alternative: Financial worry after 2008 was widespread and circumstantial.

claims.claim: When a producer told him his career was over, he says he answered "you should mind your fucking manners", walked out, and his legs gave way because "I acted so tough"; minutes later Joss Whedon called offering Vision. Later tellings vary in detail.
claims.passage: In the 2022 version, Bettany answered, "Look, this town is full of second and third acts, and you should mind your fucking manners." Then: "I walked out. My legs went because I acted so tough!"
claims.inference: Bravado in the face of a threat followed by collapse is the counterphobic Six sequence in miniature; he tells it against himself.
claims.alternative: A polished, much-repeated anecdote shaped for audiences; details shift between versions (middle finger, sitting on the pavement), so treat it as self-mythology with a stable core.

claims.claim: He has been in therapy for years ("a thousand years" by 2021-2022) and compares it to treating a chronic injury so you do not "lean back into old patterns of behavior".
claims.passage: He has been in therapy for what he called "a thousand years" ([People](https://www.yahoo.com/now/wandavision-paul-bettany-says-watching-180058582.html), 2021) and treats it as maintenance, "like having a chronic injury" that needs constant work.
claims.inference: Long reliance on a trusted support structure and maintenance mindset.
claims.alternative: Therapy use is common across types and among actors; it shows self-work, not type.

claims.claim: He says family keeps him steady: "When I'm away from them too much I begin to revert to older habits."
claims.passage: "When I'm away from them too much I begin to revert to older habits," he told the Daily Beast of his family.
claims.inference: Family as the secure base that regulates him, repeated 2013-2026.
claims.alternative: Devoted-parent statements are standard press fare and fit many types.

claims.claim: He compares himself with actors who "have amazing access to their emotions" and says "I'm just not good enough to do that."
claims.passage: "have amazing access to their emotions," adding, "And I'm just not good enough to do that," a very Four comparison.
claims.inference: Comparison with others and a sense of falling short are Four material; the article now files this line in the Four case, not as anti-Four evidence.
claims.alternative: British self-deprecation and actorly modesty; it may describe craft method rather than identity.

claims.claim: To cry on camera he describes "picking at scabs that I'd rather not pick at"; Gentleman's Journal reports he kept Matthew's sweatshirt on set for Uncle Frank.
claims.passage: "I find myself picking at scabs that I'd rather not pick at," and the magazine reported he kept Matthew's sweatshirt with him on set for a graveyard scene in _Uncle Frank_.
claims.inference: Shows he uses grief deliberately as a work tool and then questions it ("What the hell am I doing!").
claims.alternative: Using personal pain in art is a Four-compatible behaviour; the method framing is also standard actor training (Drama Centre London).

claims.claim: By Bettany's account his father Thane came out at 63 and spent about 20 years with Andy Clark, "a joyous relief for everybody".
claims.passage: By his son's account, Thane Bettany came out at 63, then spent about 20 years with a man named Andy Clark. "It was a joyous relief for everybody, actually," Bettany told Total Film in 2020,
claims.inference: A father who lived inauthentically for safety is a central family story and the background to his Uncle Frank, Warhol and VisionQuest comments.
claims.alternative: Dates conflict: Telegraph 2013 says Thane announced bisexuality "aged 75". Use Bettany's own account, attributed, and avoid exact ages beyond what he says.

claims.claim: From his father's retreat into the closet he drew a parenting rule: "I really want my children ... to just live authentically as the person they are".
claims.passage: I really want my children, and I want everybody, to just live authentically as the person they are, and however hard that is, it's absolutely better than pretending to be something other than you are.
claims.inference: Value statement; supports the Four alternative's authenticity theme and also a Six-style protective vow for the next generation.
claims.alternative: Parenting values statements in People magazine are low-cost signals.

claims.claim: Alan Ball said the film became Bettany's own 'what if' story about his father.
claims.passage: Ball later said that "for Paul, the movie became a chance for him to have his own 'what if' story about his father" (NewNowNext, relayed by Out).
claims.inference: Doubt-first engagement with an offer, then commitment once a reason is found; Ball's testimony places the motive in repairing the father story.
claims.alternative: The hesitation is partly the 2020 debate about straight actors in gay roles, which he names.

claims.claim: In October 2026 he told The Times he had not spoken to Depp in years when the texts surfaced and has not since; the close-friend portrayal struck him as 'the most odd', so he 'decided to say nothing'.
claims.passage: "I hadn't spoken to Johnny in years when that happened and I haven't spoken to him since." What struck him as "the most odd" was being "painted as this close friend of a guy I hadn't spoken to in years." "So I decided to say nothing because, I think, people know me."
claims.inference: Quoted in the source's order: 'say nothing' follows his objection to the close-friend portrayal, so it concerns not contesting that portrayal. The article draws no inconsistency from it.
claims.alternative: Ordinary crisis-PR caution. The Times original was not opened; Gulf News may have compressed the interview.
claims.review_trigger: Opening of the full 15 October 2026 Times interview; any new statement by Bettany, Depp or Heard about the texts.

claims.claim: In 2013 text messages read in Depp's 2020 UK libel case, Bettany replied to Depp's "Let's burn Amber!!!" by joking that they should instead do "a drowning test"; in 2016 he tweeted that Depp was "the sweetest, kindest, gentlest man"; since 2022 he has said they had not spoken for years and in 2026 that they have not spoken since.
claims.passage: Bettany replied, as [Insider](https://news.yahoo.com/paul-bettany-says-embarrassing-texts-111303945.html) printed it, "Having thought it through I don't think we should burn Amber — she's delightful company and easy on the eye, plus I'm not sure she's a witch. We could of course try the English course of action in these predicaments — we do a drowning test. Thoughts?"
claims.inference: The text of his reply, quoted exactly as Insider printed it. No motive is assigned.
claims.alternative: Sensitive: the texts concern a woman who alleged abuse, and Depp has denied abuse. Gulf News calls the reply 'the same mock-medieval spirit'. The article gives the UK result, the US result, the settlement, Depp's Monty Python explanation and Bettany's own later responses.
claims.review_trigger: Any new court filing, statement or reporting on the Bettany-Depp texts.

claims.claim: He has lived in the US since the early 2000s and became a US citizen.
claims.passage: who has lived in the United States since the early 2000s and became a US citizen
claims.inference: Biographical metadata only.
claims.alternative: The date of naturalisation is not established; the draft gives none.

claims.claim: He says he does 'better than I think in isolation' and is surprised he does not fall apart alone.
claims.passage: he says he does "better than I think in isolation." It surprises him: "I feel like I should fall apart more than I do. But I don't."

type_hypothesis.against: The Four case is real. Bettany speaks of alienation after Matthew's death ("harbouring some dreadful secret about what life is actually like"), measures himself against actors who "have amazing access to their emotions" ("I'm just not good enough to do that"), mines grief for performances ("picking at scabs", Matthew's sweatshirt on the Uncle Frank set), and took the authenticity lesson from his father. After Margin Call he reversed the money plan: "I need to be happy, and if that means making films for less money, so be it" (2012), the artist taking the work back. The 2026 mask answer pairs concealment with turning "very negative things into something creative" and "I can do something with this brokenness", so the mask does not separate the types. Circumstance (bullying, a sibling's death at 16, a freelance trade) explains some of the fear, and much of the record is promotional interviews in a British comic register. His 2012-2013 origin accounts stress a vocation fuelled by revenge fantasies, which the Six reading handles poorly.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 4: a man shaped by loss who feels set apart from people who have not seen "what life is actually like", compares himself unfavourably with other actors' emotional access, uses acting as a container for painful feeling, keeps returning to stories of men who could not live as themselves (Uncle Frank, Warhol, a Vision with memories he cannot feel), and prizes authenticity after watching his father retreat into the closet. Margin Call's rescue of his love for acting, the scab-picking method and the 'brokenness' line all fit. A shame-driven Four can also hide behind a role.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he does when the floor drops. A Four turns toward the loss and asks what it says about identity; a Six secures the base and pre-empts the next threat. Bettany repeatedly does the second, knowingly and at a cost: at his son's birth he decides "The world is precarious" and sets out to make the children safe "with dough", calls it ludicrous and defends it because "the tap can turn off" (2013), and says acting as a place for "terrible feelings" was "eclipsed" by that plan (2013 Guardian relay). The same worst-case framing recurs across contexts and years: fame ("What if it goes away?", 2012), money (2013), career after 2008 ("what if this thing comes tumbling down?", 2022), and, after Marvel removed the money problem, "I wonder if anybody remembers me" (2026). He copes through preparation ("the most prepared person", 2022; "pathological fear of being late", 2013) and through people and therapy. The Margin Call reversal is conceded to Four, but the worry outlived both the money years and the Marvel security. The mask/safety-net material is treated as shared ground, not as the discriminator. Type 3 was tested: self-worth from acting, 'safe and relevant', 'I was the person they remembered' and the revenge-fame fantasy invite it, but he lists judging yourself by others' praise among acting's 'terrible, terrible things', distrusts adulation, took less money after Margin Call and tells low points against himself. Type 5 (he copes alone better than expected but expects to fall apart without people) and Type 7 (he turns toward pain and death) were also tested.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: He deliberately reopens grief for work and keeps playing men who hide their true selves, which the Six reading explains only as craft. He is candid in interviews and posted political opinions on Twitter until he took US citizenship partly to stop being 'shouted down', which sits oddly with caution and with not wanting to be known 'definitively'. The revenge fantasy that, by his 2012-2013 accounts, fuelled his wish to act fits Six only as counterphobic defiance, which is thin. His 2016 public praise of Depp and his later accounts of years without contact are not reconciled in the record. The Telegraph writer, not independent research, first proposed the security/foundations frame for his marriage. Wing is not established; sociability suggests 6w7 but this is optional and unproven.
